einzeiler: How an indie filmmaking team turned their micro-budget horror debut into a theatrical…
kurzfassung: Alex Ullam, Carrie Kerrison, and Evan Barber discuss the grueling yet rewarding production journey of their indie horror feature It Ends. They explain how graduating during the pandemic led them to embrace strict limitations, rely on community support, and execute extensive reshoots. The conversation also covers creative problem-solving on a micro-budget, navigating the current distribution landscape, and building sustainable collaborations.
stichpunkte: Graduating from Florida State University into the COVID-19 pandemic inspired the team to make a micro-budget independent feature as a way to break into the industry.
Funding came from unconventional sources, including a career magician, a YouTuber, VR poker acquaintances, and a memorial film fund.
The filmmakers utilized an alumni equipment package and built scenes around severe resource constraints, shooting much of the movie on an LED volume stage.
A logistical hurdle required physically cutting a Jeep in half to fit it through a narrow studio hallway before welding it back together.
After an initial cut failed to resonate, the team embraced iterative editing and conducted extensive reshoots to tighten the pacing and blend the horror and hangout genres.
Screenings at South by Southwest eventually led to online buzz, support from Letterboxd, and a theatrical distribution deal with Neon.
The creators emphasize the value of paying crew members, meal prepping to keep production costs low, and maintaining transparent creative partnerships.

clips.text: A filmmaker humorously reflects on how his father subtly manipulated him into a career in cinema by repeatedly showing him documentaries about demanding artistic obsessions.

clips.hook: Cutting a car in half to make it fit
clips.text: The crew describes the tense moment they used a plasma torch to slice a vehicle in two so they could maneuver it around a tight studio corner.
The director candidly admits that the shortcomings of his first cut were entirely the result of his own youthful mistakes rather than external bad luck.

clips.hook: Sneaking into a major studio lot
clips.text: A filmmaker recounts jumping a fence at a studio lot, getting welcomed by security who mistook him for an influencer, and scoring free merchandise.
A producer shares a practical budgeting tactic for feeding a cast and crew affordably by preparing massive batches of frozen meals ahead of time.

beschreibung:
Writer-director Alex Ullom and producers Carrie Carusone and Evan Barber break down the unconventional path behind It Ends, their micro-budget indie horror feature about four friends trapped on an endless road. They explain how they raised their initial financing, leaned on their filmmaking community, turned production limitations into creative advantages, and used multiple rounds of strategic reshoots to transform an early cut that wasn’t working. The team also shares how they cut a Jeep in half to shoot on an LED volume stage, navigated an expensive and complicated post-production process, premiered at SXSW, and generated enough grassroots momentum through the online horror community and Letterboxd to ultimately land a theatrical release with Neon.

In this episode, No Film School's GG Hawkins and guests Alex Ullom, Carrie Carusone, and Evan Barber discuss…

How graduating from film school during the pandemic pushed the team toward making an independent feature

Raising the initial micro-budget through unconventional investors, personal connections, and community support

How Florida State University’s alumni equipment package made a $30,000 feature possible

Why paying crew something—even on an extremely limited budget—was important to the producers

Discovering in the edit that the first version of It Ends wasn’t working

Why indie filmmakers should stop thinking of reshoots as a sign of failure

Using test screenings to identify pacing problems, missing emotional beats, and scenes that needed additional coverage

Designing a contained film that could be affordably reconstructed for multiple rounds of pickups

Balancing the film’s horror and hangout-movie elements through pacing and visual language

Cutting a Jeep Cherokee in half to get it onto an LED volume stage

Rebuilding the Jeep interior and using the removable vehicle to create otherwise impossible camera angles

Why the filmmakers pulled out of Fantasia to continue improving the movie

Maintaining continuity when returning to the same actors and characters two years after principal photography

The editing workflow Alex developed to compare multiple performances of the same line

Using low-pass filtering, bass, sound design, and close-ups to create production value on an indie budget

What Alex learned from an extremely disorganized Premiere timeline

Premiering at SXSW during an especially difficult independent film distribution market

Why strong festival reviews and sold-out screenings didn’t automatically lead to a distribution deal

The changing economics of minimum guarantees for independent films

How online horror creators helped generate new momentum for It Ends

The film’s path from Letterboxd’s video store program to a theatrical release with Neon

Why filmmakers should focus on making the strongest movie possible rather than designing a project specifically for a major festival

How the lessons from It Ends changed the team’s approach to their next features

Previsualizing an entire movie before production to eliminate setups and solve story problems

Using executive producer credits strategically when raising additional financing

Practical advice for protecting hard drives, feeding a small crew, and building a trusted filmmaking community

Memorable Quotes:

“I'm a huge advocate for reshoots.”

“And on that Saturday we got it onto the stage and it, and it fit through that hallway with a literal quarter of an inch clearance on either side, and that's like, that's not an exaggeration.”

“I hope that this film can live kinda like when I first saw Slacker for the first time, and it was just like, oh, all you really need is a camera and two faces talking to each other.”

“At the end of the day, surround yourself, your entire crew with people you trust creatively.”
